raw_md:
# CRH (CRH PLC) — Value Investor Note

## Circle of Competence
Easy to understand: CRH mines aggregates, makes cement, and produces ready-mix concrete and asphalt, then sells them locally into construction and infrastructure projects. No financial engineering, no technology black box — the only real judgment call is the construction cycle itself, which is squarely within a generalist value investor's competence.

## Moat & Durability — Score 8/10
Building materials moats are geographic and physical, not brand-based: aggregates and ready-mix concrete are heavy, low value-per-ton products that are uneconomical to ship more than ~50 miles, so a quarry near a growth corridor effectively owns that radius. New-quarry permitting is now nearly impossible to obtain in most developed markets, which caps future competing supply structurally. CRH has layered scale in downstream paving/distribution on top of that raw-materials advantage since its 2023 US primary listing. This is a genuinely durable, decade-scale moat — the kind Buffett himself has bought directly (quarries, brick, and cement businesses) — docked one point only because bolt-on M&A execution risk sits on top of an otherwise structural advantage.

## Management & Capital Allocation
ROE of 15.8% on debt/equity near 78% is respectable but leverage-assisted rather than best-in-class unlevered capital efficiency. Op margin (19%) and gross margin (36.25%) both look healthy for the sector, suggesting real pricing discipline. FCF yield (3.08%) trails the P/E-implied earnings yield (~5.7%), consistent with a heavy current reinvestment cycle into capacity and bolt-on acquisitions — CRH's stated growth strategy — but this packet has no visibility into buyback pace, payout ratio, or M&A hit rate, which is the single biggest swing factor for whether this capital allocation compounds value or erodes it.

## Predictability
Revenue growth of 5.6% is moderate, but the underlying business is cyclical — tied to residential/commercial construction starts and public infrastructure spend — so it does not clear Munger's 'easy decision' bar cleanly regardless of moat quality. The market's own read is cautious rather than settled: -21.6% over six months, -12.4% below the 200-day moving average, RSI14 a neutral 51.67 (no capitulation, no euphoria), and a null thesis field leaves no additional qualitative signal. Treat predictability as moderate, constrained mainly by the construction cycle rather than the business model itself.

## Inversion — How an Owner Loses Money From Here
1. **Cyclical air pocket**: rates stay restrictive long enough that residential and commercial construction volumes fall further, compressing both units and price simultaneously — the six-month -21.6% move is the market already pricing part of this in.
2. **Leverage amplification**: debt/equity near 78% means a downturn that compresses EBITDA hits equity value disproportionately, especially while bolt-on deal commitments continue.
3. **M&A overpayment**: CRH's growth engine is aggregates/cement bolt-on acquisitions; paying up for deals late in a US infrastructure-spending cycle risks returns below the cost of capital, quietly eroding the moat's economics rather than the moat itself.

## Valuation
The packet gives market cap ($65.53B), trailing P/E (17.40x), forward P/E (14.86x), and FCF yield (3.08%) but not share count or share price. Backing into per-share terms with an approximate ~780M diluted share count (a modeling assumption, not sourced from the packet) implies a current price near $84, trailing EPS near $4.83, forward EPS near $5.65, and FCF/share near $2.59. Blending trailing EPS and FCF/share (weighted toward earnings, since current FCF looks temporarily depressed by growth capex) gives a normalized owner-earnings estimate of roughly $3.90/share.

Applying a two-stage owner-earnings model:
- **Low case** (3% long-run growth, 10% discount rate reflecting cyclicality and ~78% debt/equity): $3.90 / (0.10 − 0.03) ≈ **$56/share**.
- **High case** (4.5% growth as infrastructure spend and moat pricing power persist, 9% discount rate): $3.90 / (0.09 − 0.045) ≈ **$87/share**.

Midpoint ≈ $71.5/share against an implied current price of ≈ $84/share gives a margin of safety of roughly **-14.9%** — the stock looks modestly overvalued on a conservative owner-earnings basis despite the recent pullback, not because the business is bad but because the multiple (17.4x trailing) has not yet caught down to reflect cyclical risk and leverage.

## The Cloning Caveat
John Armitage (Egerton Capital) added to an existing position, sizing CRH at 1.68% of the portfolio — a real but non-core-conviction weight for a long/short generalist. Henry Ellenbogen (Durable Capital Partners) opened a new position at 1.6% of portfolio. Both are meaningful enough to note but far from the 20-40%+ bets that signal a manager's highest-conviction ideas — this reads as basket-level exposure to a quality cyclical at a depressed price, not a statement position. It corroborates 'this is a decent business worth watching,' not 'this is undeniably cheap right now.'

## Verdict
**Watch, conviction 5/10.** CRH owns a genuinely durable, structural moat (permitting scarcity plus transport-cost geography) in an understandable business, but the current price does not yet offer a clear margin of safety on a conservative owner-earnings basis, and elevated leverage plus M&A execution risk warrant real discount, not optimism. The right posture is to track price against the ~$56-87/share fair-value band and act if the recent downtrend (-21.6% over six months) continues into the low end of that range, rather than buying the moat story at today's implied multiple.
momentum_thesis:
CRH's momentum has flipped from a positive multi-year run into an active
breakdown: the 6-month return of -21.6% against a 12-month return of only
-6.8% means the stock was up roughly high-teens over the first half of that
window before giving it all back and then some in the back half, and it's
still sitting 12.4% below its 200DMA. RSI14 at 51.67 — neutral rather than
oversold — despite that drawdown is the tell that the 1-month print (-5.5%,
a deceleration versus the -12.7% 3-month pace) reflects exhausted selling
more than a confirmed base, so this reads as a pause inside a downtrend, not
a reversal. Positioning offers no tailwind either way: short interest is a
thin 2.4% of float with only 3.53 days to cover, so there's no squeeze fuel
to catalyze a snapback, and the put/call OI ratio at ~1.01 is essentially
flat, showing no options-market conviction on direction. The two
superinvestor moves — Egerton Capital adding 58.87% to an existing stake and
Durable Capital initiating fresh — both landed while the stock was falling
(Q1-Q2 2026), which is a valuation-driven signal, not a momentum one; it
argues these managers are underwriting the balance-sheet/cash-flow story
(forward P/E 14.9x, 15.8% ROE) ahead of price confirmation, which can mean
early and a while underwater before it means right.
